video_title: How Bitcoin Can Pay You 15% Forever
gist: Strive CEO Matt Cole explains to Anthony Pompliano how Strive sells perpetual preferred equity (13% and 15% fixed yields) as a 'perpetual dollar short' backed by Bitcoin plus a cash buffer, arguing digital credit is investment-grade risk priced like junk while traditional fixed income is broken. He also covers mandate-driven institutional access, Bitcoin as the hurdle rate, and Strive's small ETF arm as an advisor distribution channel.

themes.theme: Perpetual preferreds as a perpetual dollar short

insights.claim: Strive frames issuing perpetual preferred equity that pays a dividend forever as being perpetually short the US dollar, on the belief that the dollar will never stop being debased.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Strive's capital structure is a levered bet on fiat debasement; its preferreds and common are proxies for the debasement trade.
insights.quote: They will never stop debasing the US dollar. And so, we are perpetually short the US dollar because we are selling a perpetual preferred equity which will pay a dividend forever.

insights.claim: Strive has two perpetual preferred equities, one paying a 13% yield and one paying a 15% yield forever.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Fixed 13-15% perpetual yields set a benchmark for retail-accessible high-yield 'digital credit'.
insights.quote: One pays a 13% yield, one pays a 15% yield forever.

insights.claim: According to Matt Cole, if Bitcoin only appreciates at roughly the rate of currency debasement (about 7-8% per year), Strive can still pay its preferred dividends forever, but all Bitcoin returns would accrue to preferred holders and none to common equity; common shareholders benefit only when Bitcoin outpaces that rate.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Strive common is effectively a call on Bitcoin returns above ~13-15%; preferred holders are paid first in a low-growth Bitcoin scenario.
insights.quote: even if Bitcoin only went up around the rate of currency debasement around 7 8% per year, we could pay a dividend forever into the future.

insights.claim: Strive's primary risk is duration risk from Bitcoin volatility; it underwrites an 80% Bitcoin drawdown and holds roughly 85-90% Bitcoin and 10-15% cash so it could ride out any historical bear market without selling a single Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Cash buffer sizing is the key credit metric for digital-credit issuers; check cash coverage vs. dividend obligations.
insights.quote: we're willing to underwrite Bitcoin going down 80%. We put cash on the balance sheet.

insights.claim: Matt Cole argues Strive's no-debt, preferred-only structure has no liquidation point, claiming that even if Bitcoin went to a penny the company would have 18 months of cash to cover all obligations.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Unlike margin-levered Bitcoin positions, preferred-funded treasury companies avoid forced selling in liquidation cascades.
insights.quote: Because we have preferred equity only, no debt. We have no liquidation point.

insights.claim: Matt Cole believes Bitcoin's four-year cycles will become less meaningful in the future.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: If cycles dampen, drawdown-based underwriting may prove overly conservative, favoring levered Bitcoin vehicles.

insights.claim: Matt Cole suggests underwriting to never sell any Bitcoin in the worst historical drawdown may be too conservative, and that selling 2-5% of core assets in such a scenario would be a reasonable risk for a company.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Signals possible future loosening of Bitcoin treasury company risk buffers / higher leverage.

themes.theme: Financing stress and the broken fixed-income market

insights.claim: Matt Cole says that over the last two months CCC credit spreads have blown out by over 400 basis points, US Treasury liquidity is drying up, and data center financing costs are skyrocketing.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Widening junk spreads and costly AI data center financing signal tightening credit conditions; watch high-yield spreads and AI capex funding.
insights.quote: over the last two months triple C spreads have blown out over 400 basis points um which is wild.

insights.claim: Strive expects that over the next couple of decades financing markets becoming 'wonky' amid fiat debasement will be the trend rather than the exception, though it will play out in fits and starts.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Positions for persistently dislocated credit markets; favors issuers with no debt and perpetual funding.

insights.claim: Matt Cole agrees AI is net deflationary but argues deflation alone may not solve a sovereign debt crisis.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Don't assume AI-driven disinflation removes the debasement trade; fiscal dynamics may still force monetary debasement.

insights.claim: Matt Cole calls US Treasuries not the risk-free rate but the 'risk guaranteed rate', since holders are assured of losing real purchasing power relative to the rate of fiat currency debasement.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Frames Treasuries as a negative real-return asset vs. Bitcoin; supports rotation from traditional fixed income into hard assets / digital credit.
insights.quote: that's not the risk-free rate, that's the risk guaranteed rate

insights.claim: Matt Cole states traditional fixed income investing is fundamentally broken, with investors shunning aggregate bond funds in favor of private credit, data center financing, and (he argues) perpetual preferred equity.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Capital is migrating out of aggregate bond exposure toward alternative yield; digital credit competes with private credit for that flow.
insights.quote: our belief is that income investing is fundamentally broken.

insights.claim: Strive is built around the belief that there is an income and retirement crisis in the US within a K-shaped economy, and that the average person needs yield.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Retail yield demand is the demand driver for high-yield digital credit products.

themes.theme: Digital credit market structure and demand

insights.claim: Strive launched a second, fixed-rate junior preferred because investors were less worried about its credit risk than that the variable-rate SATA preferred would succeed so well its yield would fall to 7-8% within 3-5 years.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Investor demand is for locked-in high yields, suggesting confidence in Bitcoin-backed credit and appetite for fixed-rate perpetuals.
insights.quote: I'm uncomfortable that I'm going to end up with the thing that pays 7% and I'm not that interested in that.

insights.claim: Matt Cole predicts Strive's fixed-rate perpetual preferred will ultimately become bigger than variable-rate products like SATA or Strategy's STRC, citing that 93% of the bond market is fixed rate.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Fixed-rate digital credit may be the larger addressable market; track issuance volumes across fixed vs. variable perpetuals.
insights.quote: 93% of the bond market's fixed rate

insights.claim: Matt Cole argues digital credit is investment-grade risk if Bitcoin risk is properly underwritten, yet it is priced like junk bonds, which he calls both the reality and the opportunity.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: If the market reprices digital credit toward investment grade, yields would compress and existing fixed-rate holders gain.
insights.quote: I think digital credit is investment grade risk if you actually underwrite Bitcoin risk. It's priced like it's junk bonds.

insights.claim: About 70% of Strive's preferred investors are high-net-worth retail, while the top of the order book for its SATA offering was long-only, long-term institutional capital.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Digital credit is still retail-driven; institutional uptake is an upside catalyst for flows.

insights.claim: Institutions frequently ask Strive to repackage its perpetual preferred into a structure with term in a known wrapper, which Matt Cole says may happen in the future even though Strive itself wants no debt.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Structured products on top of digital credit could unlock institutional mandates; watch for term wrappers.

insights.claim: Matt Cole expects many more digital credit issuers because institutions face issuer caps (e.g., only 3% in Strategy or Strive while wanting 10-15% exposure) and because there is room for differentiated risk/return profiles.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Digital credit likely becomes a broad category; new issuers will appear to absorb capped institutional demand.

insights.claim: Matt Cole notes a missing digital credit product, income plus Bitcoin upside, could be issued from a corporate wrapper as return-of-capital dividends, boosting after-tax returns in a way covered-call ETFs cannot.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Corporate wrappers have tax advantages over ETFs for income products; a potential edge for Bitcoin treasury companies vs. ETF issuers.
insights.quote: in the corporate rapper, you could offer it as a return of capital dividend, which juices up the after tax returns in a way that the ETF structure never could.

themes.theme: Levered Bitcoin equity and institutional access

insights.claim: Matt Cole says many institutions cannot buy spot Bitcoin ETFs or even gold due to mandates, so preferred equity, bonds, or Bitcoin-heavy common equity provide a mandate-compliant route to Bitcoin exposure.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Mandate constraints channel institutional Bitcoin demand into treasury-company securities rather than spot.
insights.quote: a lot of institutional investors they can't even buy gold. So then you talk about digital gold and they can't buy that as well.

insights.claim: Matt Cole believes almost every institution now has an internal Bitcoiner who will push income or equity products that give Bitcoin exposure within the institution's mandate.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Bottom-up internal advocacy is an adoption vector for digital credit and Bitcoin equities.

insights.claim: Matt Cole positions Strive common equity as the best available levered Bitcoin exposure because corporate preferred financing avoids the liquidation points of traditional Bitcoin leverage that wipe out billions on each drop.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: For Bitcoin bulls seeking leverage, preferred-funded treasury equities may offer convexity without liquidation risk.

insights.claim: Strive's view on Strategy was contrary to the consensus: rather than being overlevered, Strategy was underlevered and too large to obtain the amplified exposure it wanted, so a smaller company could 'run it hotter'.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Smaller Bitcoin treasury companies may offer higher Bitcoin beta per share than Strategy.
insights.quote: the consensus criticism was that they're overlevered they're going to blow up. Our view was that they were underlevered

themes.theme: Bitcoin as the hurdle rate and portfolio allocation

insights.claim: Matt Cole argues managers should use Bitcoin as the hurdle rate because, with the dollar denominator being debased, nominal gains on S&P 500 or Treasuries may be real losses; he calls this tough hurdle a feature, not a bug.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Benchmarking against Bitcoin rather than the S&P concentrates capital in fewer themes.
insights.quote: ultimately I think that's a a feature, not a bug.

insights.claim: Matt Cole says the only areas he can get excited about are Bitcoin, AI, and energy.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Concentrated thematic focus on Bitcoin, AI and energy.
insights.quote: Bitcoin, AI, and energy. And outside of that, it's pretty hard for me to get excited about anything else.

insights.claim: Matt Cole cites modeling (including Rick Edelman's work) suggesting a 20-30% Bitcoin allocation maximizes return per unit of risk, but says BlackRock logically walked that back to 1-5% because advisers get fired when unconvinced clients see a 50% drop.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Behavioral constraints, not optimization, cap Bitcoin allocations; low-volatility wrappers expand adoption.
insights.quote: it would suggest 20 30% allocation to Bitcoin within a portfolio.

insights.claim: Matt Cole cites Bitwise's prediction of over $1 million per Bitcoin by 2036, which rests on more people adding small Bitcoin allocations.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Incremental allocations by mainstream portfolios underpin long-term price targets.
insights.quote: Bitwise's over a million dollar prediction for Bitcoin by 2036

insights.claim: Matt Cole views the new DRIP ETF (about 95% S&P, 5% Bitcoin, reinvesting dividends into Bitcoin) as adding Bitcoin too slowly but a net great product because its low volatility helps get people 'off zero' without scaring them.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Hybrid ETFs may drive slow but sticky Bitcoin adoption among unconvinced investors.
insights.quote: I think it's a net great product cuz it's not scary.

insights.claim: Strive's ETF/asset management business holds about $3 billion in assets, is at most 1% of the company's value, and is only slightly profitable; its value lies in a connection to about 7,600 advisors to whom Strive can pitch Bitcoin and digital credit.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Strive's valuation is almost entirely its Bitcoin treasury/digital credit; the ETF arm is a distribution channel.

insights.claim: Matt Cole argues large asset managers' concentrated ownership invites political pressure from both parties to vote shares in ways that harm shareholder value, a misunderstood and mispriced risk.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Proxy voting concentration is a governance risk for index-heavy portfolios.
insights.quote: I think it's misunderstood and mispriced and it creates a risk in some of the large asset managers.

insights.claim: Matt Cole says new ETF entrants cannot compete with BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street on fees, a race to zero, and must be thematic (Bitcoin, AI, energy) or offer benefits like tax-efficient rebalancing inside the wrapper; he expects fees to come down somewhat.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Differentiated thematic ETFs are the only viable wedge; expect continued fee compression.
insights.quote: That's that's a race to zero.

insights.claim: Matt Cole says fund distribution to sophisticated retail is a game of trust built by a leader going direct (e.g., weekly podcasts that nearly all Strive's largest institutional investors listen to) paired with a correct contrarian idea, rather than traditional advertising.
insights.speaker: Matt Cole
insights.so_what: Founder-led direct distribution is a durable moat for asset managers and issuers in the AI era.
